Radar absorbing materials are used to effectively absorb (with little reflection) electromagnetic energy in a certain range of radio wavelengths.
Resonant radar absorbing materials provide partial neutralization of radiation reflected from the surface when the absorber thickness is equal to one quarter of the wavelength.
Nickel ferrites are used in the ranges of mile-and centimeter waves, have high saturation magnetization and thermal stability, but high initial losses.
Magnetic ferrites are used in the middle part of the centimeter range, have low magnetic saturation but better thermal stability than nickel ferrites.
Metal screen radar absorbing materials provide good shielding efficiency at all radio frequencies, with efficiency increasing at higher frequencies.
Non-resonant bulk radar absorbing materials use both dielectric and magnetic losses to absorb incident electromagnetic energy.
Metamaterial-based radar absorbing materials can have negative magnetic permeability and electrical susceptibility, leading to negative refraction.
The example metamaterial-based absorber has a dielectric substrate with a periodic lattice of metal split-ring resonators (SRRs).
The metamaterial-based absorber can provide at least 80% absorption at incidence angles from 0 to 50 degrees at 9.5 GHz.
Smaller ferrite particle sizes (under 300 μm) allow higher effective absorption frequencies up to 12 GHz.
Metamaterial-based radar absorbing materials are being researched to improve antenna technology and noise immunity of electronic equipment.
Obtaining broadband ferrite-based absorbers is achieved by using ferrites with different resonant frequencies.
The main drawback of ferrite-based absorbers is their low manufacturability and heating from high-frequency radiation dispersion.
Metal screen absorbers have decreasing shielding efficiency at lower frequencies due to reduced absorption.
Non-resonant bulk absorbers are technologically difficult to manufacture and occupy large volumes.
